## Kisah Mahsa dan Suara Hati Iran

**Karakter:**

*   **Aisha (17 tahun):** Siswa SMA yang cerdas dan ingin tahu, selalu mencari kebenaran.
*   **Reza (16 tahun):** Teman Aisha, lebih skeptis tapi peduli dengan keadilan sosial.
*   **Pak Amir:** Guru Sejarah yang bijaksana dan selalu mendorong siswa untuk berpikir kritis.

**Adegan 1: Kelas Sejarah, Suara Hati yang Terusik**

Pagi itu, di kelas sejarah, Pak Amir memulai pelajaran dengan topik yang sedikit berbeda. Bukan tentang perang kuno atau revolusi jauh, melainkan tentang peristiwa yang sedang hangat dibicarakan di seluruh dunia: Iran.

"Anak-anak," kata Pak Amir, suaranya tenang tapi penuh makna, "siapa di antara kalian yang sudah mendengar tentang apa yang terjadi di Iran sejak September 2022?"

Beberapa siswa saling berbisik. Aisha mengangkat tangannya. "Pak, saya dengar ada banyak protes di sana. Tapi saya belum begitu paham kenapa. Ada hubungannya dengan seorang perempuan, kan?"

Pak Amir tersenyum mengangguk. "Tepat sekali, Aisha. Ini adalah kisah tentang Mahsa Amini, seorang perempuan muda berusia 22 tahun."

Reza menyahut, "Tapi apa yang terjadi padanya, Pak? Kenapa sampai jadi sebesar ini?"

"Baik," kata Pak Amir, "mari kita mulai dari awal. Mahsa Amini adalah seorang perempuan Kurdi Iran. Pada tanggal 14 September 2022, saat ia berkunjung ke Teheran dari kota asalnya, Saqqez, ia ditangkap oleh polisi moral Iran, yang dikenal sebagai 'Patroli Bimbingan'."

Aisha mengerutkan kening. "Polisi moral? Untuk apa?"

"Mereka menuduh Mahsa melanggar undang-undang wajib hijab di Iran," jelas Pak Amir. "Katanya, ia mengenakan hijabnya 'secara tidak semestinya'."

"Tidak semestinya?" Reza terdengar tidak percaya. "Hanya karena itu?"

"Ya," jawab Pak Amir, "dan sayangnya, dua hari setelah penangkapannya, pada tanggal 16 September, Mahsa Amini meninggal dunia dalam tahanan polisi."

Hening sejenak di kelas. Suasana berubah menjadi lebih serius.

"Pihak berwenang Iran bersikeras bahwa ia meninggal karena masalah kesehatan yang sudah ada sebelumnya," lanjut Pak Amir. "Namun, saksi mata dan banyak orang percaya bahwa Mahsa dipukuli secara brutal oleh petugas Patroli Bimbingan, yang menyebabkan cedera kepala fatal."

"Itu mengerikan!" seru Aisha, matanya membulat.

**Adegan 2: Api Protes yang Menyebar**

"Kematian Mahsa Amini ini," Pak Amir melanjutkan, "bukan hanya sebuah tragedi pribadi, melainkan percikan api yang menyulut kemarahan dan frustrasi yang sudah lama terpendam di masyarakat Iran."

"Jadi, apa saja tuntutan para pengunjuk rasa, Pak?" tanya Reza, mulai tertarik.

"Awalnya," kata Pak Amir, "protes dimulai di kota asal Mahsa, Saqqez, dan menyebar dengan cepat ke seluruh Kurdistan Iran, lalu ke seluruh negeri. Awalnya, sebagian besar dipimpin oleh perempuan, menuntut diakhirinya hukum wajib hijab."

Aisha mengangguk. "Tentu saja. Kalau dipaksa, itu bukan kebebasan."

"Betul," timpal Pak Amir. "Namun, seiring berjalannya waktu, tuntutan para pengunjuk rasa berkembang jauh lebih luas. Mereka bukan hanya menuntut hak-hak perempuan yang lebih besar, tetapi juga hak asasi manusia secara umum."

"Maksudnya?" tanya Reza.

"Mereka menuntut diakhirinya kekerasan dan penindasan oleh aparat keamanan, kebebasan berekspresi, dan keadilan sosial," jelas Pak Amir. "Bahkan, protes ini berkembang menjadi seruan untuk menggulingkan Republik Islam Iran itu sendiri."

"Menggulingkan pemerintah?" Aisha terkejut. "Itu tuntutan yang sangat besar."

"Memang," kata Pak Amir. "Ini menunjukkan betapa dalam dan luasnya ketidakpuasan di Iran. Tidak seperti protes-protes sebelumnya yang mungkin berfokus pada hasil pemilihan umum atau masalah ekonomi, kali ini, banyak yang menginginkan perubahan sistematis secara total."

**Adegan 3: Latar Belakang dan Respon Pemerintah**

"Untuk memahami mengapa ini terjadi," Pak Amir melanjutkan, "kita perlu melihat sedikit ke belakang. Sejak Revolusi Iran tahun 1979, perempuan diwajibkan secara hukum untuk menutup rambut mereka dengan hijab di tempat umum. Meskipun aturan ini sempat sedikit longgar di beberapa periode, penegakannya kembali diperketat di bawah Presiden Ebrahim Raisi."

"Jadi, kematian Mahsa Amini itu adalah puncak dari ketidakpuasan terhadap undang-undang ini dan penegakannya?" tanya Aisha.

"Betul sekali," jawab Pak Amir. "Selain itu, ada juga faktor-faktor lain yang memicu kemarahan, seperti kesulitan ekonomi, inflasi yang melonjak, pengangguran tinggi, korupsi, dan represi politik. Banyak orang Iran merasa masa depan mereka tidak pasti."

Reza menambahkan, "Saya dengar pemerintah Iran meresponsnya dengan sangat keras."

"Sayangnya, itu benar," kata Pak Amir dengan nada sedih. "Pemerintah Iran merespons dengan pemadaman internet yang meluas, pembatasan media sosial, penggunaan gas air mata, dan bahkan tembakan. Ribuan orang ditangkap, dan ratusan orang, termasuk anak di bawah umur, tewas dalam tindakan keras pemerintah."

Aisha menggelengkan kepalanya. "Itu mengerikan. Bagaimana bisa sebuah pemerintah melakukan itu pada rakyatnya sendiri?"

"Pemerintah Iran menganggap protes ini sebagai 'kerusuhan' dan 'perang hibrida' yang disebabkan oleh negara-negara asing," jelas Pak Amir. "Namun, kenyataannya, protes ini menyebar ke seluruh lapisan masyarakat, dari kampus hingga sekolah, dan melibatkan perempuan, termasuk anak-anak sekolah, yang memainkan peran kunci."

**Adegan 4: Suara yang Tak Terbendung**

"Meskipun ada represi yang brutal," Pak Amir menyimpulkan, "para pengunjuk rasa menunjukkan keberanian yang luar biasa. Mereka melakukan aksi 'flash mob' yang cepat dan banyak, memblokir jalan, menyanyikan slogan-slogan dari jendela, dan melakukan tindakan simbolis seperti membakar hijab atau memotong rambut mereka di depan umum."

"Mereka bahkan memboikot kelas di universitas dan melakukan mogok umum," tambah Aisha, yang sempat membaca berita.

"Tepat sekali," kata Pak Amir. "Slogan-slogan seperti 'Wanita, Kehidupan, Kebebasan' menjadi seruan yang kuat. Ini menunjukkan bahwa meskipun tantangannya besar, semangat untuk kebebasan dan keadilan di Iran tidak bisa dipadamkan."

"Jadi, intinya, Pak," kata Reza, "kematian Mahsa Amini adalah pemicu, tapi akar masalahnya lebih dalam, yaitu ketidakpuasan terhadap hukum wajib hijab, penindasan, dan kondisi hidup yang buruk, dan tuntutan utamanya adalah hak-hak perempuan, kebebasan, dan bahkan perubahan pemerintahan?"

"Kesimpulan yang sangat baik, Reza," kata Pak Amir. "Kisah Mahsa Amini dan protes di Iran adalah pengingat penting bagi kita semua tentang betapa berharganya hak asasi manusia, kebebasan, dan keadilan. Ini juga menunjukkan kekuatan kolektif masyarakat ketika mereka bersatu untuk menyuarakan ketidakpuasan mereka."

Aisha menatap teman-temannya. Ada pemahaman baru di mata mereka. Kisah Mahsa Amini bukan hanya berita jauh, tapi pelajaran tentang keberanian, penindasan, dan perjuangan abadi untuk martabat manusia.

Buat cerita edukatif yang membantu siswa memahami: What sparked the civil unrest and protests in Iran in September 2022, and what were the main demands of the protesters?

target_age: "15-18"

Context:
Civil unrest and protests against the government of Iran associated with the death in police custody of Mahsa Amini (Persian: مهسا امینی) began on 16 September 2022 and are ongoing as of July 2023. Amini had been arrested by the Guidance Patrol for allegedly violating Iran's mandatory hijab law by wearing her hijab "improperly" while visiting Tehran from Saqqez. According to eyewitnesses, she had been severely beaten by Guidance Patrol officers, an assertion denied by Iranian authorities. As the protests spread from Amini's hometown of Saqqez to other cities in the Iranian Kurdistan and throughout Iran, the government responded with widespread Internet blackouts, nationwide restrictions on social media usage, tear gas and gunfire.Although the protests have not been as deadly as those in 2019 (when more than 1,500 were killed), they have been "nationwide, spread across social classes, universities, the streets [and] schools", and called the "biggest challenge" to the government of Iran since the Islamic Revolution in 1979. At least 537 people, including 68 minors, had been killed as a result of the government's intervention in the protests, as of 4 April 2023.  An estimated 19,262 have been arrested throughout at least 134 cities and towns, and at 132 universities.Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei dismissed the widespread unrest not only as "riots" but also as a "hybrid war" caused by foreign states and dissidents abroad. Women, including schoolchildren, have played a key role in the demonstrations. In addition to demands for increased rights for women, the protests have demanded the overthrow of the Islamic Republic, setting them apart from previous major protest movements in Iran, which have focused on election results or economic woes. 
The government's response to the protests has been widely condemned.

Historical background
Since shortly after the 1979 Iranian Revolution, Iranian women have been legally required to completely cover their hair in public with a hijab. Enforcement of the unpopular law was eased during the 2013–2021 tenure of President Rouhani, but was then intensified under Rouhani's successor, the hard-line President Ebrahim Raisi.  Bloody Aban  (Persian: آبان خونین), a month near November in the Iranian calendar, was a series of 2019 protests initially caused by a 50–200% increase in fuel prices, and as part of the wider Iranian Democracy Movement, leading to calls for the overthrow of the government in Iran and Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei.

Mahsa Amini's arrest and death in custody
Mahsa Amini, a 22-year-old Kurdish Iranian woman, was arrested by the Guidance Patrol on 14 September 2022 because of an "improper hijab." The police were accused of beating her and inflicting a fatal head injury; Amini was pronounced dead on 16 September. After a CT scan confirmed that Amini had sustained head injuries, the head of the Guidance Patrol was allegedly suspended, a claim that was denied by Tehran police.

Protests
Initial protests, mostly led by women, demanded an end to the mandatory hijab; these protests evolved into a national revolt. The protests became more widespread than those of 2009, 2017, and 2019, encompassing even Islamic Republic power bases such as the holy cities of Mashhad and Qom. Unlike some previous protests, the new protests involved both urban middle classes and rural working areas. In addition, schoolgirls demonstrated in numbers for the first time. While continuing to protest Amini's death and demanding an end to the mandatory hijab, Iranians also advocated for wider freedoms and women's rights, and protested against the morality police, the Ayatollah, and the theocratic regime.Unlike many previous Iranian protests, protesters appear to be demanding a wholesale change in government rather than limiting themselves to incremental reforms. In a November 2022 Group for Analyzing and Measuring Attitudes in Iran (GAMAAN) poll, almost three-quarters of Iranians opposed mandatory hijab; of these anti-hijabis, 84% would prefer a secular Iranian state to theocracy, which GAMAAN characterized as an endorsement of regime change. According to Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty, economic hardship and poor living conditions contributed to the growth of the protests. The New York Times itemized Iranian grievances such as "soaring prices, high unemployment, corruption, (and) political repression", and identified the poor Iranian economy as a major force behind the protests; according to an Iranian report in August 2021, a third of Iranians live in poverty. Abdolreza Davari, a conservative analyst, has quoted a statistic that 95 percent of Iranians are "worried about their livelihoods today and for their and their children's future." Only 15% of Iranians in the job market are women. Iran ranked 143rd out of 146 countries in the 2022 WEF Gender Gap Report, due in part to prohibitions on female membership in powerful government organizations.In response to the protests, people held demonstrations in support of the government across several cities in Iran, in an attempt to counter the protests. The Iranian government referred to these counter-protests as "spontaneous". The pro-government protesters called for the anti-government protesters to be executed, and referred to them as "Israel's soldiers" whilst shouting "Death to America" and "Death to Israel", reflecting Iran's clerical rulers' usual narrative of putting the blame of the unrest on foreign countries.Media coverage was constrained by Iranian restrictions on speech, including Internet shutdowns and arrests of journalists. NBC News retained a correspondent in Tehran. Most Western outlets obtained information from networks of contacts, human rights groups, and social media content. According to BBC News, an Iranian government disinformation campaign produced social media videos and fake interviews, and attempted to trick Western media into reporting falsehoods: "They can then say foreign media is reporting fake news".According to France 24, protests "had dwindled" across most of the country by March 2023.

Aftermath
Events of chain poisoning in girls' schools occurred.
The state began a surveillance program.

Actions by protesters
Protesters often stage small and quick, but numerous, "flash mob" gatherings. Drivers have blocked streets with their cars to slow down security forces; roads have also been blocked by dumpster bins or even overturned police cars. Security forces on motorbikes cut through traffic, with passengers firing on protesters. In some cases security forces used paintballs to mark demonstrators; some demonstrators packed extra clothes to replace painted clothes, wore masks to avoid identification, or dismantled public security cameras. Some protesters chanted from windows or rooftops. Symbolic protests include dyeing fountains blood-red, and women discarding and burning their hijabs or cutting their hair in public. Since turbans are viewed as a symbol of the regime, some activists engaged in turban throwing (knocking the turbans off of "privileged" Iranian clerics on the street and running away); reformers such as Ahmad Zaidabadi criticized the trend, and said the practice can harass uninvolved scholars.

Civil boycotts
Some university teachers and professors declared their support for the student movement by boycotting classes or resigning. They included Nasrollah Hekmat (Shahid Beheshti University), Ammar Ashoori (Islamic Azad University), Lili Galehdaran (Shiraz Art University) and Gholamreza Shahbazi (Art and Soureh Universities), together with Alireza Bahraini, Shahram Khazaei, and Azin Movahed (Sharif University of Technology, Tehran).On December 5 to 7, 2022, a general strike took place to put pressure on the regime.

{"item_idx": 42, "source": "Myanmar civil war (2021–present)", "language": "en", "question_raw": "Question: What is the current status of the Myanmar civil war, and how many people have been internally displaced since the coup?", "question": "What is the current status of the Myanmar civil war, and how many people have been internally displaced since the coup?", "user_message": "Create an educational story that helps students understand: What is the current status of the Myanmar civil war, and how many people have been internally displaced since the coup?", "context_type": "v1+v2_merged_dedup", "merged_contexts": ["The Myanmar civil war (Burmese: ၂၀၂၁-၂၀၂၃ မြန်မာနိုင်ငံ ပြည်သူ့ခုခံတွန်းလှန်စစ်), also called the Myanmar Spring Revolution, and the People's Defensive War, is an ongoing civil war following Myanmar's long-running insurgencies which escalated significantly in response to the 2021 military coup d'état and the subsequent violent crackdown on anti-coup protests.In the months following the coup, the opposition began to coalesce around the National Unity Government, which launched an offensive against the junta. By 2022, the opposition controlled substantial, though sparsely populated, territory. In many villages and towns, the junta's attacks drove out tens of thousands of people. On the second anniversary of the coup, in February 2023, the chairman of the State Administration Council, Min Aung Hlaing, admitted to losing stable control over "more than a third" of townships. Independent observers note the real number is likely far higher, with as few as 72 out of 330 townships and all major population centres remaining under stable control.As of September 2022, 1.3 million people have been internally displaced, and over 13,000 children have been killed. By March 2023, the UN estimated that since the coup, 17.6 million people in Myanmar required humanitarian assistance, while 1.6 million were internally displaced, and 55,000 civilian buildings had been destroyed. UNOCHA said that over 40,000 people fled into neighboring countries.

Background
On the morning of 1 February 2021, the Myanmar military, or Tatmadaw, successfully deposed the elected Myanmar government in a coup, forming a military junta. Former president Win Myint, Aung San Suu Kyi, and several other members of the National League for Democracy were detained during early morning raids and Min Aung Hlaing was placed as the Commander-in-Chief of Defence Services and de facto ruler of the nation.The exact motives behind the coup are unclear. In the leadup to the coup, the Tatmadaw claimed that the 2020 general elections had 8.6 million voter irregularities, but presented no evidence. The coup may have been a way to re-establish the military's long-reigning power over the country which ended ten years prior.The bloody repression of anti-coup demonstrations led to the creation of armed groups to fight the State Administration Council, the military junta. Gathered under the name of the People's Defence Force (PDF) and the orders of the National Unity Government (NUG), formed by former parliamentarians in office before the coup d'état, the PDF and the NUG officially declared a "defensive war" against the military regime in September 2021. The ACLED estimated that as of 29 July 2022, around 23,521 people in total had been killed in the violence following the 2021 coup.

Existing conflict
Insurgencies have been ongoing in Myanmar since 1948 and have largely been ethnic-based. Communist insurgencies and the Karen National Union were the primary opposition actors to the central government. Over the 20th century, several prominent ethnic armed organisations (EAOs) rose and fell in influence and control. Larger rebel factions such as the Kachin Independence Army formed in response to Ne Win's 1962 Burmese coup d'état and its increased political repression. The 8888 Uprising in response to the totalitarian rule of Ne Win resulted in some of the first modern Bamar militias forming from protestors heading to areas under ethnic rebel control.
In the aftermath of the 8888 Uprising, the State Law and Order Restoration Council, later called the State Peace and Development Council, formed a military junta. The Tatmadaw severely weakened ethnic insurgent groups, destroying most of their bases and strongholds through the 1990s. By the time of the 2011–2015 Myanmar political reforms, the junta had regained control of many long-time rebel strongholds including Kokang and Karen State.As part of its political reforms and democratization, the 2008 Constitution created self-administered zones with increased autonomy. In 2015, the Nationwide Ceasefire Agreement (NCA) was signed between 8 EAOs and the central government. However, as soon as 2018, the NCA had already begun to fall apart due to alleged violations of the agreement by Tatmadaw soldiers entering EAO territories to build roads. Many non-signatories continued the conflict. In late 2016, four non-signatories of the NCA formed the Northern Alliance, including the Kachin Independence Army and Arakan Army, engaged in war with the central government and other EAOs.

Prelude
Armed protestors
In late March, dozens of protesters had travelled to Myanmar's border areas to enlist in and train under one of the country's many insurgent groups, elevating the risk of a countrywide civil war. The Committee Representing Pyidaungsu Hluttaw also proposed the formation of a "federal armed force" to combat the military, and in late March the Arakan Army (AA) threatened to end its ceasefire with the military should the latter "persist in massacring civilians".During late March, protesters increasingly began arming themselves with homemade weapons such as guns in an attempt to defend themselves against attacks by the military. Simultaneously, clashes with soldiers and IED attacks against administrative buildings and police stations became more common as the trend of protesters using armed resistance rose.

Renewed ethnic conflict
The unrest across the nation and the increased need for junta troops in previously peaceful urban areas strengthened EAOs. The Kachin Independence Army (KIA) has already been on the offensive against the military since February and seized the military base of Alaw Bum near the town of Laiza on 25 March. The next day, the Karen National Liberation Army (KNLA) attacked a military base, killing 10 soldiers and taking others hostages in the first attack on the military since the protests began. The following day saw the 2021 Kalay clashes, the first openly armed resistance by protesters in the town of Kalay against the junta. Protestors used homemade weapons against soldiers and security forces attacking a protest camp.The military junta declared that it would cease all military operations on 29 March and hold bilateral negotiations with ethnic armed groups. However, the KIA continued its offensives stating that the Myanmar Army had continued operations as usual. Through April, the informal clashes intensified, such as on 8 April when protesters fought back against soldiers with hunting rifles and firebombs in a battle that resulted in 11 protesters' deaths. The same day, the country surpassed 600 deaths related to anti-coup protests since 1 February.Seven insurgent groups who were signatories to the Nationwide Ceasefire Agreement aligned themselves with the Committee Representing Pyidaungsu Hluttaw, including the All Burma Student Democratic Front and the Karen National Union. The Northern Alliance, comprising the Arakan Army, the Ta'ang National Liberation Army and the Myanmar National Democratic Alliance Army, attacked a police station in Naungmon, Shan State, killing at least 10 police officers and indicating their disregard of the junta's call for a ceasefire. In response, on 11 April, the junta military launched a counter-attack to recapture the Alaw Bum base using airstrikes and ground troops, but had to retreat amidst heavy casualties.

New conflicts
On 26 April, the Battle of Mindat became one of the first large-scale conflicts arising from the 2021 coup. The Chinland Defense Force (CDF) began armed resistance in Mindat, Chin State. As a response, the junta cut off food and water supplies and declared martial law. Fighting began when a group of demonstrators outside the town's Aung San statue requested the release of six of their arrested colleagues, when a soldier of the regime allegedly fired at someone, prompting protesters to react.
According to an aid worker, more than 10,000 people have left Mindat in southern Chin State as the Myanmar military star", "violently. The situation quickly escalated into a full-blown clash between the military and the protesters.

The military, armed with heavy weaponry and supported by armored vehicles, launched a brutal crackdown on the demonstrators. Tear gas, rubber bullets, and live ammunition were used indiscriminately, resulting in numerous casualties among the protesters. The streets of the town turned into a chaotic battleground, with fires burning and the sound of gunfire echoing through the air.

Despite the overwhelming force of the military, the protesters fought back with whatever they could find. They threw rocks, Molotov cocktails, and set up makeshift barricades to slow down the advancing troops. The clashes continued for hours, with both sides sustaining heavy losses.

As news of the violent clashes spread, more people from neighboring towns and villages joined the protest, swelling the ranks of the demonstrators. The military's attempts to quell the uprising only fueled the people's anger and determination to fight for their rights and freedom.

International condemnation poured in as reports of the brutal crackdown reached the global community. Calls for an immediate end to the violence and the release of all political prisoners grew louder. Diplomatic pressure was exerted on the junta, with sanctions and other punitive measures threatened if the violence did not cease.

Inside the town, the fighting raged on. The protesters, fueled by their desire for justice and democracy, refused to back down. They formed a network of underground resistance, organizing protests, strikes, and acts of civil disobedience to disrupt the military's control.

The junta, realizing the growing resistance and international pressure, eventually agreed to enter into negotiations with the protesters. A ceasefire was declared, and talks began to find a peaceful resolution to the crisis. However, the trust between the two sides was shattered, and the road to reconciliation would be long and arduous.

The town's Aung San statue, once a symbol of hope and unity, now stood as a reminder of the violence and bloodshed that had taken place. The scars of the conflict would take time to heal, but the people's determination to fight for their rights remained unbroken. They knew that the struggle for democracy was far from over, and they were willing to continue the fight, no matter the cost."]}

{"final_story": "The classroom buzzed with the usual Friday afternoon energy, but today, Mr. Harrison had a different kind of story to tell. He dimmed the lights, drawing the students’ attention to the large screen behind him. On it, a map of Southeast Asia glowed, with Myanmar highlighted in a vibrant red.

“Today, we’re going to talk about a country facing immense challenges, a place where people are fighting for their basic rights and safety: Myanmar,” Mr. Harrison began, his voice calm but serious. “For generations, Myanmar has experienced periods of conflict. But what we’re focusing on today is the current situation, which escalated dramatically after a military coup in February 2021.”

He clicked to a slide showing a timeline. “Imagine waking up one morning to find your elected government overthrown, your leaders arrested, and the military back in charge,” Mr. Harrison explained. “That’s what happened on February 1st, 2021, when the Myanmar military, known as the Tatmadaw, seized power from the civilian government.”

A student named Maya raised her hand. “Why did they do that, Mr. Harrison?”

“Good question, Maya. The Tatmadaw claimed the 2020 elections were fraudulent, but they offered no solid proof. Many believe it was a move to re-establish their long-held power, which they had seemingly relinquished a decade earlier during a period of reforms,” he replied, highlighting the complexities.

He then showed images of peaceful protests being met with brutal force: water cannons, tear gas, and even live ammunition. “This crackdown on peaceful anti-coup demonstrations ignited something fierce in the people. They refused to accept the military’s rule,” Mr. Harrison continued. “This widespread resistance eventually morphed into what many call the ‘Myanmar Spring Revolution’ or the ‘People’s Defensive War’.”

“So, it’s not really *one* civil war, but more like a series of conflicts?” asked Chen, thoughtfully.

“That’s a brilliant way to put it, Chen,” Mr. Harrison nodded. “Myanmar has a long history of insurgencies, often ethnic-based, some dating back to its independence in 1948. And crucial to understanding the current situation, many of those older ethnic armed groups (EAOs) that had been fighting the military for decades, some even aligning with the NUG, also intensified their offensives.”

“So, what’s the current status of this war?” asked Liam, leaning forward.

Mr. Harrison switched to a current map of Myanmar. “The situation is fragmented and constantly evolving, Liam. More than 55,000 civilian buildings have been destroyed,” Mr. Harrison added, the statistics painting a stark picture. “Furthermore, over 40,000 people have fled across borders into neighboring countries, seeking refuge.”

“So, there’s no end in sight?” asked Chen, his brow furrowed.

“The future is uncertain, Chen. The military junta faces widespread resistance, both armed and through civil disobedience. The conflict is incredibly complex, with a long history, and many different groups involved. What we do know is that the people of Myanmar are enduring immense suffering, and the global community continues to watch, hoping for a peaceful resolution and the restoration of democracy. It’s a powerful reminder of the fragility of peace and the devastating consequences when it’s shattered.”

Mr. Harrison turned the lights back on, the map of Myanmar still glowing on the screen, a silent testament to the ongoing struggle. The classroom, which had been buzzing moments before, was now hushed, the students grappling with the weight of the story he had shared. Create an educational story that helps students understand: What is the current status of the Myanmar civil war, and how many people have been internally displaced since the coup?

target_age: "15-18"
story_style: "educational"
language: "English"

Context:
The Myanmar civil war (Burmese: ၂၀၂၁-၂၀၂၃ မြန်မာနိုင်ငံ ပြည်သူ့ခုခံတွန်းလှန်စစ်), also called the Myanmar Spring Revolution, and the People's Defensive War, is an ongoing civil war following Myanmar's long-running insurgencies which escalated significantly in response to the 2021 military coup d'état and the subsequent violent crackdown on anti-coup protests.In the months following the coup, the opposition began to coalesce around the National Unity Government, which launched an offensive against the junta. By 2022, the opposition controlled substantial, though sparsely populated, territory. In many villages and towns, the junta's attacks drove out tens of thousands of people. On the second anniversary of the coup, in February 2023, the chairman of the State Administration Council, Min Aung Hlaing, admitted to losing stable control over "more than a third" of townships. Independent observers note the real number is likely far higher, with as few as 72 out of 330 townships and all major population centres remaining under stable control.As of September 2022, 1.3 million people have been internally displaced, and over 13,000 children have been killed. By March 2023, the UN estimated that since the coup, 17.6 million people in Myanmar required humanitarian assistance, while 1.6 million were internally displaced, and 55,000 civilian buildings had been destroyed. UNOCHA said that over 40,000 people fled into neighboring countries.

Background
On the morning of 1 February 2021, the Myanmar military, or Tatmadaw, successfully deposed the elected Myanmar government in a coup, forming a military junta. Former president Win Myint, Aung San Suu Kyi, and several other members of the National League for Democracy were detained during early morning raids and Min Aung Hlaing was placed as the Commander-in-Chief of Defence Services and de facto ruler of the nation.The exact motives behind the coup are unclear. In the leadup to the coup, the Tatmadaw claimed that the 2020 general elections had 8.6 million voter irregularities, but presented no evidence. The coup may have been a way to re-establish the military's long-reigning power over the country which ended ten years prior.The bloody repression of anti-coup demonstrations led to the creation of armed groups to fight the State Administration Council, the military junta. Gathered under the name of the People's Defence Force (PDF) and the orders of the National Unity Government (NUG), formed by former parliamentarians in office before the coup d'état, the PDF and the NUG officially declared a "defensive war" against the military regime in September 2021. The ACLED estimated that as of 29 July 2022, around 23,521 people in total had been killed in the violence following the 2021 coup.

Existing conflict
Insurgencies have been ongoing in Myanmar since 1948 and have largely been ethnic-based. Communist insurgencies and the Karen National Union were the primary opposition actors to the central government. Over the 20th century, several prominent ethnic armed organisations (EAOs) rose and fell in influence and control. Larger rebel factions such as the Kachin Independence Army formed in response to Ne Win's 1962 Burmese coup d'état and its increased political repression. The 8888 Uprising in response to the totalitarian rule of Ne Win resulted in some of the first modern Bamar militias forming from protestors heading to areas under ethnic rebel control.
In the aftermath of the 8888 Uprising, the State Law and Order Restoration Council, later called the State Peace and Development Council, formed a military junta. The Tatmadaw severely weakened ethnic insurgent groups, destroying most of their bases and strongholds through the 1990s. By the time of the 2011–2015 Myanmar political reforms, the junta had regained control of many long-time rebel strongholds including Kokang and Karen State.As part of its political reforms and democratization, the 2008 Constitution created self-administered zones with increased autonomy. In 2015, the Nationwide Ceasefire Agreement (NCA) was signed between 8 EAOs and the central government. However, as soon as 2018, the NCA had already begun to fall apart due to alleged violations of the agreement by Tatmadaw soldiers entering EAO territories to build roads. Many non-signatories continued the conflict. In late 2016, four non-signatories of the NCA formed the Northern Alliance, including the Kachin Independence Army and Arakan Army, engaged in war with the central government and other EAOs.

Prelude
Armed protestors
In late March, dozens of protesters had travelled to Myanmar's border areas to enlist in and train under one of the country's many insurgent groups, elevating the risk of a countrywide civil war. The Committee Representing Pyidaungsu Hluttaw also proposed the formation of a "federal armed force" to combat the military, and in late March the Arakan Army (AA) threatened to end its ceasefire with the military should the latter "persist in massacring civilians".During late March, protesters increasingly began arming themselves with homemade weapons such as guns in an attempt to defend themselves against attacks by the military. Simultaneously, clashes with soldiers and IED attacks against administrative buildings and police stations became more common as the trend of protesters using armed resistance rose.

Renewed ethnic conflict
The unrest across the nation and the increased need for junta troops in previously peaceful urban areas strengthened EAOs. The Kachin Independence Army (KIA) has already been on the offensive against the military since February and seized the military base of Alaw Bum near the town of Laiza on 25 March. The next day, the Karen National Liberation Army (KNLA) attacked a military base, killing 10 soldiers and taking others hostages in the first attack on the military since the protests began. The following day saw the 2021 Kalay clashes, the first openly armed resistance by protesters in the town of Kalay against the junta. Protestors used homemade weapons against soldiers and security forces attacking a protest camp.The military junta declared that it would cease all military operations on 29 March and hold bilateral negotiations with ethnic armed groups. However, the KIA continued its offensives stating that the Myanmar Army had continued operations as usual. Through April, the informal clashes intensified, such as on 8 April when protesters fought back against soldiers with hunting rifles and firebombs in a battle that resulted in 11 protesters' deaths. The same day, the country surpassed 600 deaths related to anti-coup protests since 1 February.Seven insurgent groups who were signatories to the Nationwide Ceasefire Agreement aligned themselves with the Committee Representing Pyidaungsu Hluttaw, including the All Burma Student Democratic Front and the Karen National Union. The Northern Alliance, comprising the Arakan Army, the Ta'ang National Liberation Army and the Myanmar National Democratic Alliance Army, attacked a police station in Naungmon, Shan State, killing at least 10 police officers and indicating their disregard of the junta's call for a ceasefire. In response, on 11 April, the junta military launched a counter-attack to recapture the Alaw Bum base using airstrikes and ground troops, but had to retreat amidst heavy casualties.

New conflicts
On 26 April, the Battle of Mindat became one of the first large-scale conflicts arising from the 2021 coup. The Chinland Defense Force (CDF) began armed resistance in Mindat, Chin State. As a response, the junta cut off food and water supplies and declared martial law. Fighting began when a group of demonstrators outside the town's Aung San statue requested the release of six of their arrested colleagues, when a soldier of the regime allegedly fired at someone, prompting protesters to react.
According to an aid worker, more than 10,000 people have left Mindat in southern Chin State as the Myanmar military star

violently. The situation quickly escalated into a full-blown clash between the military and the protesters.

The military, armed with heavy weaponry and supported by armored vehicles, launched a brutal crackdown on the demonstrators. Tear gas, rubber bullets, and live ammunition were used indiscriminately, resulting in numerous casualties among the protesters. The streets of the town turned into a chaotic battleground, with fires burning and the sound of gunfire echoing through the air.

Despite the overwhelming force of the military, the protesters fought back with whatever they could find. They threw rocks, Molotov cocktails, and set up makeshift barricades to slow down the advancing troops. The clashes continued for hours, with both sides sustaining heavy losses.

As news of the violent clashes spread, more people from neighboring towns and villages joined the protest, swelling the ranks of the demonstrators. The military's attempts to quell the uprising only fueled the people's anger and determination to fight for their rights and freedom.

International condemnation poured in as reports of the brutal crackdown reached the global community. Calls for an immediate end to the violence and the release of all political prisoners grew louder. Diplomatic pressure was exerted on the junta, with sanctions and other punitive measures threatened if the violence did not cease.

Inside the town, the fighting raged on. The protesters, fueled by their desire for justice and democracy, refused to back down. They formed a network of underground resistance, organizing protests, strikes, and acts of civil disobedience to disrupt the military's control.

The junta, realizing the growing resistance and international pressure, eventually agreed to enter into negotiations with the protesters. A ceasefire was declared, and talks began to find a peaceful resolution to the crisis. However, the trust between the two sides was shattered, and the road to reconciliation would be long and arduous.

The town's Aung San statue, once a symbol of hope and unity, now stood as a reminder of the violence and bloodshed that had taken place. The scars of the conflict would take time to heal, but the people's determination to fight for their rights remained unbroken. They knew that the struggle for democracy was far from over, and they were willing to continue the fight, no matter the cost.

---

## Kisah Nicholas, Si Penggali Akar dan Jendela Waktu Iklim

**Tokoh:**

*   **Nicholas (Nick):** Seorang siswa SMA yang cerdas dan selalu ingin tahu.
*   **Bu Dewi:** Guru Geografi Nick yang berwawasan luas dan inspiratif.
*   **Pak Bima:** Seorang klimatolog, kerabat Bu Dewi yang suka bercerita.

**Bagian 1: Sebuah Artikel yang Membingungkan**

Pagi itu, di kelas Geografi, Bu Dewi membagikan sebuah artikel ilmiah yang berjudul "Beyond the Comfort Zone: The Human Climate Niche and Our Future." Nick membaca judulnya dengan kerutan di dahi. "Niche iklim manusia? Apa itu, Bu?" tanyanya, mewakili rasa penasaran teman-temannya.

Bu Dewi tersenyum. "Pertanyaan bagus, Nick. Niche iklim manusia itu bukan sekadar suhu ruangan yang nyaman untuk kita tinggal. Ini lebih dalam dari itu. Ini adalah keseluruhan kondisi iklim – suhu, curah hujan, dan lain-lain – yang telah memungkinkan manusia untuk berkembang biak, bercocok tanam, dan membangun peradaban selama ribuan tahun terakhir di Bumi."

"Jadi, kita punya 'zona nyaman' iklim global?" tanya Maya, teman Nick.

"Tepat sekali, Maya," jawab Bu Dewi. "Dan yang menarik, para ilmuwan bisa *mengestimasi* niche iklim ini. Caranya adalah dengan melihat di mana populasi manusia padat di seluruh dunia dan menghubungkannya dengan suhu rata-rata tahunan di daerah tersebut."

Nick berpikir, "Bagaimana bisa suhu rata-rata tahunan saja menjadi kunci untuk mengukur niche sebesar itu?"

Bu Dewi menjelaskan, "Bayangkan begini, Nick. Para ilmuwan mengumpulkan data populasi manusia dari berbagai belahan dunia. Lalu, mereka memplot data itu terhadap suhu rata-rata tahunan di lokasi-lokasi tersebut. Hasilnya sangat menarik. Distribusi populasi itu membentuk dua puncak yang signifikan."

"Dua puncak?" Nick semakin penasaran.

**Bagian 2: Jendela Waktu dan Prediksi Masa Depan**

Bu Dewi melanjutkan, "Nah, yang menjadi masalah adalah perubahan iklim global. Dengan meningkatnya suhu rata-rata Bumi, kita diproyeksikan akan mengalami kondisi iklim yang berada *di luar* niche iklim manusia ini."

"Persis, Nick. Beberapa proyeksi menunjukkan bahwa, dengan mempertimbangkan perubahan suhu dan pertumbuhan populasi, 2 miliar orang pada tahun 2030 dan bahkan 3.7 miliar orang pada tahun 2090 akan hidup di luar kondisi niche iklim yang selama ini mendukung kehidupan dan peradaban kita."

"Tunggu, Bu," Maya menyela. "Apakah itu berarti kita harus pindah semua ke daerah yang lebih dingin?"

"Itu salah satu opsi, Maya, meskipun tidak realistis untuk miliaran orang," jawab Bu Dewi. "Intinya adalah, kita harus beradaptasi. Adaptasi perubahan iklim adalah proses menyesuaikan diri dengan dampak perubahan iklim. Baik dampak yang sedang terjadi maupun yang akan datang."

**Bagian 3: Piknik ke Rumah Klimatolog**

Untuk membantu siswa lebih memahami, Bu Dewi mengumumkan, "Ada kerabat saya, Pak Bima, seorang klimatolog. Beliau punya kebun percobaan dan banyak cerita menarik. Bagaimana kalau kita berkunjung akhir pekan ini?" Seluruh kelas bersorak gembira.

"Apakah ada strategi adaptasi yang konkret, Pak?" tanya Rizal.

"Tentu saja! Ada banyak cara. Misalnya:

1.  **Membangun infrastruktur tahan iklim:** Bayangkan rumah-rumah yang didesain untuk menahan panas ekstrem atau banjir, atau tanggul yang kuat untuk melindungi dari kenaikan permukaan air laut.
2.  **Mengembangkan pertanian pintar iklim:** Menggunakan varietas tanaman yang tahan kekeringan atau banjir, atau teknologi irigasi tetes yang hemat air. Di kebun Bapak ini, saya sedang mencoba beberapa varietas tomat yang tahan suhu tinggi. Dulunya, tomat tidak bisa tumbuh bagus di suhu lebih dari 30 derajat Celcius, tapi sekarang para peneliti mengembangkan jenis baru.
3.  **Sistem peringatan dini:** Untuk bencana seperti kekeringan atau badai.
4.  **Mengelola sumber daya air lebih bijaksana:** Panen air hujan, desalinasi, atau mendaur ulang air.
5.  **Membantu ekosistem beradaptasi:** Menanam kembali hutan bakau untuk melindungi pesisir, atau menciptakan koridor hijau agar satwa liar bisa berpindah ke daerah yang lebih sesuai. Manusia juga bisa beradaptasi secara alami, seperti yang dilakukan banyak penduduk di daerah panas, mereka beristirahat di tengah hari dan beraktivitas saat pagi atau sore.

"Intinya," Pak Bima melanjutkan, "adaptasi itu tentang membuat kita dan alam bisa bertahan dan bahkan berkembang dalam kondisi iklim yang berubah. Tujuannya adalah mengurangi kerugian dan memaksimalkan potensi positif."

Nick mengangkat tangan. "Jadi, niche iklim manusia itu bukan batasan yang kaku, Pak? Kita bisa memperluasnya dengan adaptasi?"

"Pertanyaan yang brilian, Nick!" puji Pak Bima. "Niche alami itu memang ada, dan itu menunjukkan preferensi kita. Tapi, sebagai manusia, kita punya kemampuan luar biasa untuk berinovasi dan beradaptasi. Dengan ilmu pengetahuan dan teknologi, kita bisa 'merekayasa' lingkungan kita, sampai batas tertentu, untuk tetap nyaman di tengah perubahan. Namun, ingat, ada batasnya. Kita tidak bisa terus-menerus melawan alam tanpa konsekuensi."

Bu Dewi menyimpulkan, "Pelajaran hari ini adalah: kita telah mengidentifikasi 'zona nyaman' iklim kita selama ribuan tahun. Perubahan iklim mengancam membuat kita keluar dari zona itu. Tapi, dengan pemahaman, inovasi, dan kerja sama, kita bisa mengembangkan strategi adaptasi yang cerdas untuk melindungi diri kita, serta peluang yang ada, demi masa depan yang lebih baik. Kalian semua adalah generasi yang akan menjadi arsitek adaptasi tersebut."

Nick dan teman-temannya saling pandang, pemahaman baru menyelimuti benak mereka. Kisah tentang niche iklim dan tantangan adaptasi kini punya makna yang jauh lebih dalam. Mereka bukan hanya menerima informasi, tetapi juga merasa terpanggil untuk menjadi bagian dari solusi.

metadata.user_prompt:
Buat cerita edukatif yang membantu siswa memahami: What is the human climate niche and how is it estimated?

target_age: "15-18"
story_style: "educational"
language: "Indonesian"

Context:
The human climate niche is the ensemble of climate conditions that have sustained human life and human activities, like agriculture, on the globe for the last millennia. The human climate niche is estimated by calculating the human population density with respect to mean annual temperature. The human population distribution as a function of mean annual temperature is bimodal and results in two modes; one at 15 °C and another one at ∼20 to 25 °C. Crops and livestock required for sustaining the human population are also limited to the similar niche conditions. Given the rise in mean global temperatures, the human population is projected to experience climate conditions beyond the human climate niche. Some projections show that considering temperature and demographic changes, 2.0 and 3.7 billion people will live in out of the niche by 2030 and 2090, respectively.

Climate change adaptation is the process of adjusting to the effects of climate change. These can be both current or expected impacts.[1] Adaptation aims to moderate or avoid harm for people. It also aims to exploit opportunities. Humans may also intervene to help adjustment for natural systems.[1] There are many adaptation strategies or options.They can help manage impacts and risks to people and nature.

However, it was later subjected to Russia's unilateral annexation of southeastern Ukraine, and remains under direct Russian control as of 10 May 2023.
During the Russian siege, the Red Cross described the situation in Mariupol as "apocalyptic" while Ukrainian authorities accused Russia of engineering a major humanitarian crisis in the city. Ukrainian officials reported that approximately 25,000 civilians had been killed and that at least 95% of the city had been destroyed during the fighting, primarily by large-scale Russian bombardments. In an official statement, the United Nations confirmed the deaths of 1,348 civilians in Mariupol, but warned that the true death toll was likely thousands higher while also reporting that 90% of the city's residential buildings had been damaged or completely destroyed.Major combat operations in the city effectively ended on 16 May 2022 after Ukraine's Azov Regiment surrendered at the Azovstal Iron and Steel Works. However, the loss of the city has also been seen as a significant defeat for Ukraine.

It was the largest city in the Ukrainian-controlled portion of Donetsk Oblast, and was also one of the largest Russian-speaking cities in Ukraine. {"final_story": "The chilly March wind whipped around Anya’s face, carrying with it the scent of ash and the distant, rhythmic thud of artillery. She clutched her worn textbook tighter against her chest, the words on the page a blur compared to the stark reality outside the makeshift classroom. Mr. Petrov, their history teacher, cleared his throat, pulling them back from their individual anxieties.

“Alright, class,” he began, his voice calm despite the flickering candlelight. “Today, we’re going to discuss a chapter in our recent history that, while difficult, is crucial to understand. We’re talking about the Siege of Mariupol.”

A hush fell over the students. Many of them had family or friends who had lived in Mariupol, or had seen the devastating images on news channels that occasionally flickered to life.

“To understand the siege,” Mr. Petrov continued, “we first need to go back a little. Mariupol, as you know, is a vital port city on the Sea of Azov in Ukraine’s Donetsk Oblast. It was a major industrial hub, home to places like the Azovstal Iron and Steel Works, and a significant economic center. Its strategic importance was immense, especially for access to the Sea of Azov and as a potential land bridge to Crimea. This strategic value had made it a target before, even back in 2014, when the Donetsk People's Republic briefly controlled it before Ukrainian forces recaptured it. There were even rocket attacks in 2015 and a tense naval incident in 2018. So, the city was no stranger to conflict.”

He paused, letting the information sink in. “Now, fast forward to February 24th, 2022, the day the full-scale Russian invasion of Ukraine began. On that very day, Mariupol came under attack. Russian forces, advancing from the east, began bombarding the city and attempting to encircle it.”

He projected a map onto the wall, highlighting the city’s location and the surrounding Russian advances. “Initially, Ukrainian forces, including brave soldiers from the Azov Regiment – a group with its own complex history, but instrumental in defending the city – managed to repel some early attacks. However, by March 2nd, the situation changed dramatically. Russian and DPR forces had fully surrounded Mariupol.”

Natalia, a quiet girl in the front row, raised her hand. “Mr. Petrov, you said it was surrounded. How long did it stay like that?”

Mr. Petrov nodded. “Excellent question, Natalia. This is where the sheer duration of the siege becomes truly harrowing. From that day, March 2nd, the city was completely cut off. The siege of Mariupol, from the initial attacks on February 24th, 2022, lasted for a staggering **almost three months.** It didn't end until **May 20th, 2022.** Think about that. Day after day, for nearly ninety days, a city of hundreds of thousands was under constant attack, besieged.”

He showed them some satellite images of the city, before and after. The contrast was stark – vibrant streets reduced to rubble, once-majestic buildings now skeletal remains.

“During this period,” Mr. Petrov’s voice grew somber, “the situation inside Mariupol became apocalyptic, as described by organizations like the Red Cross. Electricity, gas, water, internet – all cut off. Civilians had no escape, trapped in a relentless bombardment. Ukrainian officials reported horrific numbers, estimating around 25,000 civilians had been killed. The United Nations, while confirming 1,348 deaths, warned that the true toll was likely thousands higher. And the city itself? At least 95% of it was destroyed. Over 90% of residential buildings were damaged or completely ruined. The scale of destruction was immense, primarily due to large-scale Russian bombardments.”

A collective gasp went through the room. The reality of those numbers, the sheer devastation, was difficult to comprehend.

“And what was the outcome, Mr. Petrov?” asked Oleksiy, his brow furrowed.

“The siege ended with Mariupol falling under Russian control,” Mr. Petrov stated plainly. “The last significant pockets of resistance were the Ukrainian troops, many of whom were sheltering in the sprawling Azovstal Iron and Steel Works. These brave defenders, after being ordered to cease fighting, finally surrendered on May 20th, 2022. This marked the end of Ukraine’s control over the city.

He then presented a complex nuance. “Now, the outcome is viewed in different ways. For Russia and the Donetsk People's Republic, it was a victory. They achieved their strategic objective of securing a land route to Crimea and gaining full control over the Sea of Azov. And for Russia, it was also symbolic, given their stated goal of 'denazification,' and the Azov Regiment’s controversial presence there.

However, many Western reports described it as a ‘pyrrhic victory’ – a victory achieved at such a great cost that it’s almost like a defeat. Others called it a 'reputational disaster' for Russia due to the humanitarian catastrophe it caused. For Ukraine, the loss of Mariupol was undoubtedly a significant defeat, both strategically and symbolically. It stripped Ukraine of its largest city in Donetsk Oblast and a vital port.

After the surrender, Mariupol was initially controlled by the Donetsk People's Republic, supported by Russian forces. Then, it was subjected to Russia’s unilateral annexation of southeastern Ukraine and remains under direct Russian control to this day.”

Mr. Petrov turned off the projector, plunging the room back into the soft candlelight. “The Siege of Mariupol was a brutal, extended conflict that highlights the devastating consequences of war on civilians and urban centers. It lasted for nearly three months, from the first day of the invasion on February 24th to May 20th, 2022. The outcome was the capture of the city by Russian forces, but at an almost unimaginable cost in human lives and widespread destruction. It’s a stark reminder of the sacrifices made and the profound impact of this conflict on the people of Ukraine.”

Anya looked down at her textbook, the words now carrying a much heavier weight. Context:
The Siege of Mariupol began on 24 February 2022 and lasted until 20 May, as part of the Russian invasion of Ukraine. It saw fighting between the Russian Armed Forces (alongside the Donetsk People's Republic People's Militia) and the Ukrainian Armed Forces for control over Mariupol. Lasting for almost three months, the siege ended in a victory for Russia and the Donetsk People's Republic, as Ukraine lost control of the city amidst Russia's eastern Ukraine offensive and southern Ukraine offensive; all Ukrainian troops remaining in the city surrendered at the Azovstal Iron and Steel Works on 20 May 2022, after they were ordered to cease fighting.Mariupol is located in Ukraine's Donetsk Oblast, and following the siege, it was initially controlled by the Donetsk People's Republic, supported by occupying Russian troops. However, it was later subjected to Russia's unilateral annexation of southeastern Ukraine, and remains under direct Russian control as of 10 May 2023.
During the Russian siege, the Red Cross described the situation in Mariupol as "apocalyptic" while Ukrainian authorities accused Russia of engineering a major humanitarian crisis in the city. Ukrainian officials reported that approximately 25,000 civilians had been killed and that at least 95% of the city had been destroyed during the fighting, primarily by large-scale Russian bombardments. In an official statement, the United Nations confirmed the deaths of 1,348 civilians in Mariupol, but warned that the true death toll was likely thousands higher while also reporting that 90% of the city's residential buildings had been damaged or completely destroyed.Major combat operations in the city effectively ended on 16 May 2022 after Ukraine's Azov Regiment surrendered at the Azovstal Iron and Steel Works. Some Western reports described the siege as a pyrrhic or symbolic Russian victory, with others noting that the humanitarian impact of the takeover was a "reputational disaster" for Russia. However, the loss of the city has also been seen as a significant defeat for Ukraine.

Background
Mariupol was considered a major strategic city and therefore was a target for Russian forces. It was the largest city in the Ukrainian-controlled portion of Donetsk Oblast, and was also one of the largest Russian-speaking cities in Ukraine. Mariupol was a major industrial hub, home of the Illich and Azovstal Iron and Steel Works, and the largest city on the Sea of Azov.Control of its port on the western shore of the Sea of Azov is vital to the economy of Ukraine. For Russia, it would allow a land route to Crimea and allow passage by Russian marine traffic. Capturing the city gave Russia full control over the Sea of Azov.In 2014 after the Revolution of Dignity, Mariupol was swept by pro-Russian protests against the new government. Tensions erupted into the war in Donbas in early May, and during the unrest, militiamen of the separatist and Russian-backed Donetsk People's Republic (DPR) took control of the city and forced Ukrainian troops to abandon it during the first battle for Mariupol. However, the following month, Ukrainian forces recaptured the city in an offensive. In August, the DPR and Russian troops captured the village of Novoazovsk, 45 km east of Mariupol near the Russo-Ukrainian border. With the town captured and forces renewed, in September the DPR attempted to capture the city again in the second battle for Mariupol. Fighting reached the eastern outskirts, but the separatists were eventually repelled. In October, then-DPR Prime Minister Alexander Zakharchenko vowed to retake the city. Mariupol was then indiscriminately bombed by rockets in January 2015. Fearing a future third offensive into Mariupol, in February Ukrainian forces launched a surprise attack into Shyrokyne, a village located 11 km east of Mariupol with the objective of expelling the separatist forces from the city limits and creating a buffer zone. The separatists withdrew from Shyrokyne four months later. The conflict was frozen when the Minsk II ceasefire agreement was signed in 2015.2018 saw again tension in the region around Mariupol, as the Russian Federal Security Service (FSB) coast guard fired upon and captured three Ukrainian Navy vessels after they attempted to transit from the Black Sea into the Sea of Azov through the Kerch Strait on their way to the port of Mariupol. The Kerch Strait incident raised tensions, and martial law was briefly declared by Ukraine in fears that a war would break out between the two countries.One of the most instrumental groups for the recapture and subsequent defenses of Mariupol was the Azov Battalion, a Ukrainian volunteer militia, controversial for its openly neo-Nazi and ultranationalist members. By November 2014 Azov was integrated into the National Guard of Ukraine, with Mariupol as its headquarters. As one of Vladimir Putin's stated goals for the invasion was the "denazification" of Ukraine, Mariupol represented an important ideological and symbolical target for the Russian forces.Prior to the siege, around 100,000 residents left Mariupol, according to the city's deputy mayor.Prior to falling to Russian forces, the city was defended by the Ukrainian Ground Forces, the Ukrainian Naval Infantry, the National Guard of Ukraine (primarily the Azov Regiment), the Territorial Defense Forces of Ukraine, and irregular forces.

Preliminary shelling and advance on the city
On 24 February, the day the invasion began, Russian artillery bombarded the city, reportedly injuring 26 people.On the morning of 25 February, Russian forces advanced from DPR territory in the east towards Mariupol. They encountered Ukrainian forces near the village of Pavlopil, whom repelled the Russian advance. The mayor of Mariupol, Vadym Boychenko, said 22 Russian tanks had been destroyed in the skirmish. That evening, the Russian Navy, drawing on the capabilities provided by the Black Sea Fleet, reportedly began an amphibious assault on the Sea of Azov coastline 70 kilometres (43 mi) west of Mariupol. A US defense official stated that the Russians may have deployed thousands of marines from this beachhead.On 26 February, Russian forces continued to bombard Mariupol with artillery. Later, the government of Greece announced that ten ethnic Greek civilians had been killed by Russian strikes at Mariupol, six in the village of Sartana and four in the village of Buhas.On the morning of 27 February, mayor Boychenko said that a Russian tank column had advanced on Mariupol from the DPR, but this attack was repulsed by Ukrainian forces, with six Russian soldiers captured. Later that day, a 6-year-old girl in Mariupol was killed by Russian shelling. Pavlo Kyrylenko, governor of Donetsk Oblast, stated that fighting in Mariupol had continued throughout the night of 27 February.Throughout 28 February, the city remained under Ukrainian control despite being surrounded by Russian troops and constantly shelled. Electricity, gas, and internet connection to most of the city was cut during the evening. On 1 March, Denis Pushilin, the head of the DPR, announced that DPR forces had almost completely surrounded the nearby city of Volnovakha and that they would soon do the same to Mariupol. Boychenko announced the city was suffering from a water outage and had experienced massive casualties. He also said Russian forces were preventing civilians from exiting.

Tariq nodded, his throat dry. "Indeed, sir. I can only imagine what it must have been like centuries ago, before… well, before there were even clear paths."

The old man chuckled, a dry, raspy sound. "Ah, but there *were* paths, Tariq. And one of the most remarkable was built precisely to ease the suffering of pilgrims like us. Have you ever heard of the Zubaydah Trail?"

Tariq shook his head. "I don't think so."

"Then let me tell you a story," the old man began, leaning back against a sun-baked rock. "A story of perseverance, faith, and a queen who left an enduring legacy."

But even then, the journey to the holy cities of Mecca and Medina was fraught with peril. Tribes and traders had always crisscrossed these lands, following ancient routes to find water and sustenance. These were informal paths, often difficult to navigate, especially for large groups of pilgrims."

"So, when was this Zubaydah Trail constructed, then?" Tariq asked, intrigued.

"It wasn't a single event, like building a house," the old man explained. "Think of it more as a grand project that unfolded over many centuries. The Abbasid Caliphate itself began in **132 AH, which is around 750 CE**. And this monumental undertaking, the construction and enhancement of the Zubaydah Trail, continued throughout their reign, right up until **656 AH, or 1258 CE**. She was the daughter of Caliph Abu Ja'far al-Mansur and, crucially, the wife of the legendary Caliph Harun al-Rashid. You see, in **176 AH**, Queen Zubaydah herself embarked on the Hajj pilgrimage. And let me tell you, Tariq, she experienced firsthand the immense hardships of that journey."

"She saw the suffering of pilgrims, the lack of reliable water, the scorching sun, and the treacherous terrain. It deeply moved her. And unlike many, she didn't just lament the situation; she acted. She, along with her husband, dedicated a significant portion of their immense wealth to improving the pilgrimage route. She ordered the construction of well-organized rest areas, strategically placed ponds to collect precious rainwater, and even canals to channel water. She understood that a safe and accessible path was not just a convenience, but a necessity for the faithful."

"So, the trail existed before her, but she transformed it?" Tariq clarified.

"Precisely!" the old man affirmed. "The route itself had been used for centuries, even before Islam, by various tribes and merchants. It was a natural corridor between Iraq and Western Arabia. Over time, as those ancient water sources and grazing lands became more established, they naturally became stopping points. But it was during the Abbasid era, and largely thanks to Queen Zubaydah's vision and dedication, that this informal path became a meticulously planned and engineered highway of faith."

"The Abbasid Caliphs, recognizing the importance of the Hajj, took a keen interest in this route. They weren't just building a road; they were building a lifeline. Along this vast distance, they established **27 main stations**, like small towns, providing shelter and supplies. And between these main stations, every 50 kilometers or so, they built **58 subsidiary stations, called Muta'asha**, which were essential rest stops."

"They didn't just build a path, Tariq. They engineered a wonder. In sandy and muddy areas, they paved the surface with stones. They dug wells, built dams, and constructed ponds to ensure a constant supply of water. They even put up signposts, lighthouses, beacons, and stoves to mark the way and guide travelers, even at night."

Tariq looked around at the barren landscape, then back at the old man. "It's hard to imagine such a sophisticated infrastructure in such a remote area, so long ago."

"That, my boy, is the genius of it," the old man said with a smile. "The Zubaydah Trail, also known as the Al-Kufi pilgrimage route, is one of seven major pilgrimage routes in the Arabian Peninsula. The late afternoon sun cast long shadows across the bustling cafeteria of “Academia Global,” but inside, a buzz of excitement was focused on a screensaver: a vibrant picture of a young woman in a sparkling gown, holding a golden scepter.

"Alright, class, settle down, settle down!" Mrs. Elena, their civic engagement teacher, clapped her hands. "Today, we're going to talk about an event that celebrates our nation's beauty, talent, and passion for peace: the Miss Grand Dominican Republic pageant!"

A few students exchanged glances. Pageants? Some thought they were old-fashioned, others found them glamorous. But Mrs. Elena had a knack for making any topic interesting.

"First things first," she began, her eyes sparkling, "let's clear up some questions. David, I saw you eyeing that picture. When and where will the Miss Grand Dominican Republic 2023 pageant be held?"

David, usually quick with answers, paused. "Um, I… I think I saw something online… Is it in August?"

"Excellent start, David! It is indeed on **August 4, 2023**," Mrs. Elena confirmed, pulling up a dynamic presentation with images of the Dominican Republic. "And the spectacular venue for this year's competition will be the **Cibao Grand Theatre in Santiago de los Caballeros**."

A collective murmur went through the class. "Santiago? That's a big deal!" Mariana exclaimed. "Is it always there?"

"Not always, Mariana," Mrs. Elena replied. "This is only the second edition of the Miss Grand Dominican Republic pageant. It's still relatively new in its current format. This year is particularly exciting because it's the first time it’s being managed by a new team, Alejandro Martínez and Jorge Cruz, after they took over the license."

Carlos, a budding journalist, raised his hand. "Mrs. Elena, I've heard the name Alejandro Martínez before. Didn't he and Jorge Cruz also direct another pageant called Misses of Dominican Republic?"

"You've done your research, Carlos! That's absolutely correct," Mrs. Elena praised. "They have a lot of experience in the pageant world, having previously sent our representatives to international competitions like Miss Grand International, Miss Asia Pacific International, and Miss Supranational in 2021. Their expertise is a great asset for Miss Grand Dominican Republic."

"But… why *this* pageant?" asked Sofia, always wanting to understand the deeper meaning. "What's the purpose of the Miss Grand Dominican Republic pageant?"

Mrs. Elena smiled, knowing this was the most crucial question. "That, Sofia, is the heart of it. The primary purpose of the Miss Grand Dominican Republic pageant is to **select a representative to compete on the international stage at Miss Grand International 2023.**"

She then projected a map of Vietnam. "This year, the international competition, Miss Grand International 2023, is scheduled to be held in **Vietnam on October 25th.** Our winner will travel there to proudly represent our beautiful country."

"So, it’s not just about looking pretty?" Leo, a sports enthusiast, asked skeptically.

"Far from it, Leo!" Mrs. Elena emphasized. "While beauty is certainly a component, pageants like Miss Grand International emphasize much more. "Wow," Sofia breathed, looking at the picture of the golden scepter again, but with new eyes. "So, the Dominican Republic is sending someone to advocate for world peace?"

"Precisely!" Mrs. Elena confirmed. "Our candidate will join women from all over the world, not just to showcase her grace and intelligence, but also to lend her voice to this vital cause. In fact, the Dominican Republic has a special history with Miss Grand International. We even won the title once in 2015 with Anea Garcia, though she was later replaced."

She continued, "This year, we have nine confirmed candidates from various parts of our country, each bringing her unique background and passion to the competition. For example, we have Asia Ciaffarafa representing Distrito Nacional, Andreina Santos from the Dominican communities in the USA, and Skarxi Marie representing Santiago, the host city. Each of these women will compete for the honor of wearing that golden crown and carrying the 'Stop the War and Violence' message to Vietnam."

"So, these women are more than just models," Carlos mused, taking notes. "They're ambassadors."

"Exactly, Carlos," Mrs. Elena affirmed. "They are representatives of our culture, our spirit, and our commitment to a better world. They are competing for the chance to unite voices and inspire change on a global scale. So, when you hear about the Miss Grand Dominican Republic 2023 pageant on August 4th at the Cibao Grand Theatre, remember that it's not just a beauty contest, but a platform for a powerful message of peace from our incredible nation."

{"item_idx": 34, "source": "2022 Hormozgan earthquakes", "language": "id", "question_raw": "Question: How many people were killed and injured in the 2022 Hormozgan earthquakes, and what was the maximum intensity of the earthquakes?", "question": "How many people were killed and injured in the 2022 Hormozgan earthquakes, and what was the maximum intensity of the earthquakes?", "user_message": "Buat cerita edukatif yang membantu siswa memahami: How many people were killed and injured in the 2022 Hormozgan earthquakes, and what was the maximum intensity of the earthquakes?", "context_type": "v1+v2_merged_dedup", "merged_contexts": ["The 2022 Hormozgan earthquakes were a pair of doublet earthquakes that struck southern Iran on 1 July, 2022. The earthquakes, which occurred around two hours apart, killed seven people and injured dozens more.

Tectonic setting
Hormozgan province lies at the southern margin of the collision zone between the Eurasian Plate and the Arabian Plate. This collision lead to the creation of the Zagros Mountains and the Iranian Plateau. The main fault system that runs through the Zagros Range is the Zagros fold and thrust belt, which has been responsible for causing many earthquakes in Iran over the years.

Earthquake
This earthquake is part of a sequence of earthquakes on 1 July, 2022, in southern Iran that began with a magnitude 6.0, followed by a magnitude 5.7 aftershock two hours later, and a magnitude 6.0 earthquake one minute after the magnitude 5.7 earthquake. The first two events were initially reported as 6.1 magnitude, while the third was an initial 6.2. They were revised down several hours later. Earthquake sequences similar to this one have previously occurred in the Zagros Mountains, with a similar sequence occurring in November 2021.

Aftershocks
By 3 July, there were twelve aftershocks, the strongest of which was 5.7 Mw. On July 23, two more aftershocks occurred, measuring 5.4 and 5.6 Mw . The two quakes caused further damage to houses, and caused one indirect injury.

Intensity
The earthquakes had a maximum intensity of VII (Very strong). The strongest shaking was reported in the provinces of Hormozgan and Fars. The earthquake was felt throughout the Middle East in countries such as the United Arab Emirates, Oman, Saudi Arabia, Bahrain and Qatar, as well as parts of Pakistan and Afghanistan, which were severely affected by a more deadly earthquake 10 days earlier.

Other events
Two offshore earthquakes occurred in the same province near the town of Kish a month before the July events. The earthquakes measured 5.5 and 5.6 on the moment magnitude scale, and occurred at a depth of 10.0 km. The first earthquake injured four and damaged 20 buildings. The latter caused one death and 37 injuries.Another earthquake, measuring magnitude 5.9 struck the same area on March 16 of that same year. It caused two injuries and minor damage in several villages.

Impact
Twelve towns and over 300 villages, with a combined population of around 900,000, were impacted by the earthquakes. The village of Sayeh Khvosh, home to around 1,100 people, was completely destroyed. The governor of Hormozgan, Mahdi Dousti, said that it would take several months to rebuild the village. In Bandar Khamir, at least 45 houses were affected, and 35 others were damaged in the town of Kong. In total, at least 392 houses were damaged or destroyed. There were also reports of power outages. A road between Bandar Khamir and Bandar Lengeh was blocked by a landslide. Seven people were killed and 111 others were injured. At least 22 of the injuries were serious enough to require hospitalisation.

{"final_story": "Tentu, ini dia cerita edukatif tentang gempa bumi Hormozgan 2022 yang ditujukan untuk siswa usia 15-18 tahun:

## Kisah Gempa Ganda Hormozgan: Pelajaran dari Bumi yang Bergeser

**Karakter:**

*   **Aisha:** Siswa SMA yang tertarik pada geografi dan bencana alam.
*   **Pak Budi:** Guru Geografi Aisha yang berpengetahuan luas.
*   **Narator:** Suara yang memandu cerita.

---

**Narator:** Di sebuah kelas Geografi yang cerah, Aisha dengan cermat mendengarkan Pak Budi menjelaskan tentang lempeng tektonik. Hari itu, topik diskusi mereka adalah peristiwa gempa bumi yang baru-baru ini terjadi, khususnya di Hormozgan, Iran.

**Pak Budi:** "Anak-anak, seperti yang kita pelajari, bumi kita ini dinamis. Lempeng-lempeng raksasa terus bergerak, dan terkadang, pergerakan itu menyebabkan gempa bumi yang dahsyat. Hari ini, kita akan membahas Gempa Bumi Hormozgan 2022 sebagai studi kasus yang penting."

**Aisha:** (Mengacungkan tangan) "Pak, saya membaca sekilas beritanya. Gempa itu terjadi di Iran, kan? Apakah itu gempa tunggal atau ada beberapa gempa?"

**Pak Budi:** "Pertanyaan yang bagus, Aisha! Gempa Hormozgan 2022 ini sangat menarik karena merupakan **gempa ganda (doublet earthquakes)**. Bayangkan, ada dua gempa besar yang terjadi hanya dalam waktu sekitar dua jam! Ini terjadi pada tanggal 1 Juli 2022 di Iran selatan."

**Narator:** Pak Budi kemudian menampilkan peta di proyektor, menunjukkan lokasi Provinsi Hormozgan di Iran.

**Pak Budi:** "Provinsi Hormozgan ini terletak di daerah yang sangat aktif secara geologis. Ini adalah batas selatan zona tumbukan antara Lempeng Eurasia dan Lempeng Arab. Tumbukan inilah yang membentuk Pegunungan Zagros yang megah dan Dataran Tinggi Iran. Jadi, daerah ini memang langganan gempa."

**Aisha:** "Jadi, gempa itu besar, ya, Pak? Seberapa besar?"

**Pak Budi:** "Awalnya, laporan menyebutkan gempa pertama berkekuatan 6.1 M dan gempa kedua 6.2 M. Tapi setelah dianalisis lebih lanjut, para ahli merevisi kekuatan gempa-gempa tersebut. Urutannya begini: gempa pertama berkekuatan **Magnitudo 6.0**, lalu disusul gempa susulan berkekuatan 5.7 M dua jam kemudian, dan hanya satu menit setelah gempa 5.7 M itu, terjadi lagi gempa berkekuatan **Magnitudo 6.0**! Urutan gempa seperti ini, di mana ada gempa utama diikuti gempa susulan dan kemudian gempa utama lagi, sering terjadi di Pegunungan Zagros."

**Narator:** Aisha mencatat dengan teliti. Ia mulai menyadari kompleksitas peristiwa gempa bumi.

**Aisha:** "Lalu, Pak, berapa banyak korban jiwa dan luka-luka akibat gempa ganda ini?"

**Pak Budi:** "Ini adalah bagian yang paling menyedihkan, Aisha. Gempa ganda ini menyebabkan **tujuh orang meninggal dunia**. Selain itu, **seratus sebelas orang lainnya mengalami luka-luka**. Dari jumlah yang terluka, setidaknya 22 orang cukup serius sehingga membutuhkan rawat inap di rumah sakit."

**Aisha:** "Betapa mengerikannya! Dan seberapa kuat getaran yang dirasakan, Pak? Apakah ada skala untuk mengukurnya?"

**Pak Budi:** "Tentu saja ada. Kita menggunakan skala intensitas untuk mengukur seberapa kuat getaran dirasakan di permukaan bumi dan dampaknya. Gempa Hormozgan ini memiliki **intensitas maksimum VII (Sangat Kuat)**. Getaran terkuat dilaporkan terjadi di provinsi Hormozgan dan Fars. Bahkan, gempa ini terasa hingga ke berbagai negara di Timur Tengah seperti Uni Emirat Arab, Oman, Arab Saudi, Bahrain, Qatar, serta sebagian Pakistan dan Afghanistan."

**Narator:** Pak Budi melanjutkan penjelasannya, menunjukkan gambar-gambar dampak gempa.

**Pak Budi:** "Dampak gempa ini sangat signifikan. Dua belas kota dan lebih dari 300 desa, dengan total populasi sekitar 900.000 jiwa, terkena dampaknya. Desa Sayeh Khvosh, yang dihuni sekitar 1.100 orang, bahkan hancur total. Gubernur Hormozgan mengatakan butuh waktu berbulan-bulan untuk membangun kembali desa itu. Total, setidaknya 392 rumah rusak atau hancur."

**Aisha:** "Jadi, Pak, untuk merangkumnya, jika ada yang bertanya tentang Gempa Hormozgan 2022: **Berapa banyak orang yang meninggal dan terluka, dan berapa intensitas maksimum gempa tersebut?**"

**Pak Budi:** "Tepat sekali, Aisha! Jawaban singkatnya adalah:
*   **Tujuh orang meninggal dunia.**
*   **Seratus sebelas orang terluka.**
*   **Intensitas maksimum gempa adalah VII (Sangat Kuat).**

**Pak Budi:** "Penting untuk diingat bahwa gempa bumi adalah pengingat kuat akan kekuatan alam. Memahami bagaimana gempa terjadi, dampaknya, dan cara kita meresponsnya adalah bagian penting dari literasi geografi. Semoga kisah ini memberi kalian pemahaman yang lebih dalam."
